title: Matthew 28:11–15
context: While the women go with Easter news, some of the guard report to the chief priests. The leaders bribe the soldiers to spread a theft story, promise protection from the governor, and a rival account takes root that Matthew says persists to his day.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on while the women go with Easter news, some of the guard report to the chief priests—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Matthew 28:11–15.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Say, his disciples came by night, and stole him while we slept - Is it possible, that any man of sense should digest this poor, shallow inconsistency? If ye were awake, why did you let the disciples steal him?
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 28:11–15)

reformed.quote: It is not only credible, but the fact is manifest, that the soldiers, to whom had been entrusted the charge of the sepulcher, were corrupted by a bribe, so that they were prepared to tell a lie at the bidding of the priests. They knew well that there was nothing which the priests dreaded more than that a report should gain credit that Christ rose on the third day after his death; and they knew that they had been sent there, that, by guarding the body, they might suppress that report.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 28:11–15)

verses.text: While they were going, behold, some of the guard went into the city and told the chief priests all that had taken place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Parallel paths: women run with truth; guards report “all that had taken place” to priests. Facts reach the council even as gospel runs to disciples.

Arminian warning: knowledge of events is not repentance. Hearing what happened at the tomb can still harden into damage control instead of faith.
verses.reformedNotes:
Providence lets soldiers carry news to the same leaders who sealed the tomb. “All that had taken place” enters hostile ears.

Reformed sobriety: God’s act is not hidden from opponents. The question becomes what sinners do with undeniable disturbance.

verses.text: And when they had assembled with the elders and taken counsel, they gave a sufficient sum of money to the soldiers
verses.arminianNotes:
Assembly, counsel, cash—religion manages crisis by bribery. A “sufficient sum” buys a story. Silver again stains holy office.

Arminian application: hearts can prefer paid narrative over living Christ. Grace still calls leaders to truth; counsel without conversion invents cover.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elders join priests; money follows counsel. Institutional power tries to purchase silence about resurrection.

Reformed clarity: human plotting is real and culpable. God’s risen Son is not undone by a budget line for false witness.

verses.text: and said, “Tell people, ‘His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The official line is absurd by design: sleeping guards who somehow know thieves were disciples. Lie upon lie to blunt Easter.

Arminian pastoral: unbelief often prefers a story it can control. Grace invites honest facing of the empty tomb; this counsel invites people to swallow contradiction rather than trust Christ.
verses.reformedNotes:
Theft-while-asleep is the council’s catechism for the public. False witness is commissioned as policy.

Reformed diagnosis: suppressing resurrection truth is active sin. The alternative narrative exposes how far hard hearts will go.
verses.keyContrast: Both reject the theft tale as dishonest. Arminians typically press how resistible light is smothered by chosen falsehood; Reformed readers typically press the culpability of leaders under providence that still lets the true word advance.

verses.text: And if this comes to the governor’s ears, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Political cover is promised: we will satisfy the governor. Fear of Rome is managed so fear of God need not be faced.

Arminian edge: security without truth is a cruel kindness. Grace offers a better protection—the risen Lord—than elite patronage over a lie.
verses.reformedNotes:
Soldiers are shielded from Pilate if the story leaks. Earthly power underwrites the fiction.

Reformed note: the world’s peacekeeping can become partnership in deceit. God’s court will weigh both the bribe and the promise to “satisfy” men.

verses.text: So they took the money and did as they were directed. And this story has been spread among the Jews to this day.
verses.arminianNotes:
Money taken; directions followed; rumor spreads “to this day.” Matthew refuses to pretend everyone believed. Competing stories endure.

Arminian urgency: persistence of a false account does not make it true. Grace still sets the empty tomb and the living Christ before every generation that hears both tales.
verses.reformedNotes:
Compliance is bought; the rumor has staying power. Scripture records the counter-gospel without fear.

Reformed confidence: God’s Word names the lie and outlasts it. The church confesses resurrection not because propaganda vanished, but because Christ lives.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat the lasting rumor as real history and false explanation. Arminians typically urge a fresh, responsible turn from propaganda to the risen Lord; Reformed readers typically stress God’s preservation of true witness amid enduring opposition He foreknew.
